Definition: Percentage of individuals who used the internet (from any location, via any device) in the last three months. This measures actual internet adoption beyond network availability, capturing the combined effect of infrastructure, affordability, digital literacy, and relevance.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. ITU/FRED puts internet use at 36.8% (2024) and DataReportal at 35.1% (Jan 2025); a 2024 secondary estimate (Africarrieres) gives 43.8%. All estimates fall within the 30-49% band. Value Code 3 confirmed.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: NOT CONFIRMED — flag for human review. The cited 94.2% figure is GSMA's cellular mobile CONNECTIONS (SIM count) as a share of population, explicitly noted by DataReportal itself to overstate unique users because of multi-SIM ownership; it does not measure the 'unique mobile subscriber penetration' this variable requires. No country-specific unique-subscriber percentage could be verified. Corroborating context (GSMA Mobile Connectivity Index places Mali in the lowest 'Discoverers' tier, score 33.9, alongside Liberia and Mozambique) suggests true unique-subscriber penetration is materially lower than 70%+. Could not find an authoritative unique-subscriber figure; do not treat Code 5 as confirmed.

Value Name: Served remotely from distant regions only (>100ms latency)
Comments: Distant remote only, no local hyperscale [[BMC](https://www.bmc.com/blogs/aws-vs-azure-vs-google-cloud-platforms/)]
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Original source (a generic BMC blog comparing AWS/Azure/GCP) does not mention Mali and is unrelated to the country — flagged. Verified instead via AWS's region list (nearest hyperscale presence is af-south-1, Cape Town, and Google Cloud's africa-south1, Johannesburg — both a different sub-region from landlocked West African Mali) and a colocation directory describing Mali's market as 'emerging' with only limited local infrastructure and no confirmed hyperscale presence. Code 2 (served remotely from distant regions) confirmed, but with a corrected source.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted comprehensive data protection and privacy legislation. A foundational legal requirement for building trust in digital public infrastructure and for enabling secure cross-border data flows under frameworks like the AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection.
Value Name: Legislation enacted with Data Protection Authority established
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed via the primary legal text (Law No. 2013-015 of 21 May 2013, published on the Malian Prime Minister's office site and the telecoms regulator AMRTP) and independent trackers, which confirm the APDP supervisory authority was established by the law and became operational in 2016. Code 4 confirmed with stronger, primary sourcing than the original aggregator link.

Definition: The presence and tier quality of commercial/colocation data center facilities operating in the country. Commercial data centers provide the physical infrastructure for hosting cloud services, content delivery, and enterprise applications domestically.
Comments: Sovereign Tier III data center inaugurated [[Broadcast Media Africa](https://news.broadcastmediaafrica.com/2026/02/03/mali-paves-the-way-for-digital-sovereign-tier-iii-data-centre-deployment/)]
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Flag for human review — code left unchanged. Multiple outlets (DataCenterDynamics, ITWeb Africa, TechAfrica News, Ecofin Agency) confirm a Tier III-standard facility opened in Bamako on 31 January 2026, but all describe it explicitly as a GOVERNMENT/sovereign National Data Centre for hosting state data and e-government platforms, not a commercial colocation facility open to third parties (this variable's definition). A colocation-market directory still describes Mali's commercial/colocation sector as 'emerging' with limited infrastructure. The distinction between this government facility and 'commercial' presence needs confirming before any upgrade; recommend human review of whether the National Data Centre offers third-party colocation.

Value Name: National data center operational with cloud strategy adopted
Comments: National Tier III Data Centre operational [[Broadcast Media Africa](https://news.broadcastmediaafrica.com/2026/02/03/mali-paves-the-way-for-digital-sovereign-tier-iii-data-centre-deployment/)]

revision_notes: Confirmed and well corroborated (previously single-sourced). Mali's Ministry of Communication, Digital Economy and Administrative Modernisation launched a Tier III-standard 'National Data Centre' in Bamako on 31 January 2026, explicitly for hosting state data, e-government platforms and public digital services as part of a stated digital-sovereignty strategy, with a gradual repatriation of data hosted abroad under way. Code 4 confirmed via four independent outlets (DCD, ITWeb Africa, Ecofin, TechAfrica News).

Definition: Frequency and severity of power outages experienced by businesses and households. Based on World Bank Enterprise Surveys, Afrobarometer, or national utility data. Reflects the quality of electricity supply beyond mere access — critical for running ICT equipment and data infrastructure.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Changed from Code 2 to Code 1. The cited Enterprise Survey PDF could not be fully verified for the specific 26.6/month figure, and Mali's electricity utility (EDM) has been in an acute, sustained crisis since late 2023: multiple independent news sources report near-daily nationwide load shedding of 6-18 hours a day, with households in Bamako reduced to just 4-6 hours of supply as recently as November 2025. This is 'frequent daily outages or regular load shedding' — the top of the severity scale — not 'weekly, intermittent' as originally scored.

Definition: Percentage of total electricity generation from renewable sources (hydro, solar, wind, geothermal, biomass). Indicates energy sustainability and potential for distributed power solutions relevant to ICT infrastructure in off-grid areas.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Changed from Code 2 to Code 3. The original figure (5.7%) is non-hydro renewables only, not total renewable share as the variable requires, and is a mismatch with the code selected. EIA-sourced data (via TheGlobalEconomy) shows hydropower alone was 38.2% of generation in 2023 (down from ~40-46% in 2017-2021); EDM's own director-general stated in March 2024 that thermal (fossil) generation had risen to around 70% of output (from 17% two decades ago) due to the fuel/financial crisis, implying a renewable (mostly hydro) share of roughly 25-30%. This places total renewable generation in the 25-49% band, not 10-24%; recommend confirming the precise current-year IRENA figure given the fast-moving energy crisis.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Changed from Code 2 to Code 1. Even the original 2019 figures cited (91% urban / 15% rural = 76pp gap) do not match the Code 2 band (41-60pp) that was assigned — this was already a scoring error. Updated World Bank data for 2023 (mirrored via CountryDataHub) shows urban access at 91.5% and rural access at 22.7%, a gap of 68.8 percentage points, which is 'Gap >60pp', i.e. Code 1.

Definition: The maturity of the country's technology startup ecosystem, based on the number of tech startups, venture capital activity, accelerators/incubators, and the presence of a supportive ecosystem. Africa's startup scene is well-documented by trackers like Partech, Disrupt Africa, and Briter Bridges.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Partech's 2025 Africa report does not list Mali among named ecosystems (Kenya, South Africa, Egypt, Nigeria, then Senegal/Morocco/Ghana as the next tier over $50M), consistent with a small, early-stage market. Verified deal activity is modest: Mali-linked climate-insurtech OKO raised an undisclosed six-figure round in October 2025 (after a $1.2m seed in 2021), and the newly launched Orange Corners Innovation Fund Mali disbursed circa €100k across three startups in November 2025. A widely-circulated $50m 2024 Mali figure (from a secondary blog, afric.news) is not corroborated by the primary Partech report and should be disregarded. 'Emerging, limited funding' (Code 2) confirmed.

revision_notes: Changed from Code 2 to Code 3. The 2019 source is out of date. AfriLabs' current Mali country page lists Impact Hub Bamako, Jokkolabs Mali and Nyetaa Mali (Business Innovation and Incubation Centre), plus Expert'labs Mali; a 2024/2026 sector guide additionally names Orange Digital Center Mali, Sahel Innovation, Blue Bees, YELEMAN, Mali TechHub, Ndomo Tech Hub and the UNINOVA university incubator. This is at least 8-10 identifiable hubs, well beyond '1-2', supporting '3-9 hubs with regular activity' (Code 3); activity levels of every listed hub were not individually verified, so a more generous Code 4 was not assigned.
